newsitem.title: UK: UK"s Clarke pledges no change in EMU policy.
newsitem.headline: UK"s Clarke pledges no change in EMU policy.

text.p: British finance minister Kenneth Clarke on Wednesday pledged the Conservative government would fight the next election without changing its "wait and see" policy on joining a European single currency.
But he doubted if European monetary union (EMU) would go ahead as scheduled on January 1, 1999.
Clarke, one of the fiercest pro-Europeans in a deeply divided party, was facing a bruising two-day debate in parliament over Britain's future ties with the European Union.
"The sensible thing is not to try and close down one side of the choice at this stage," Clarke told BBC Radio.

"Eurosceptics", who accuse Brussels of encroaching on Britain's national sovereignty, have called for Clarke's resignation and urged Prime Minister John Major to turn his back on the single currency negotiations.

Major, whose one-seat parliamentary majority vanished when a disaffected Conservative parliamentarian withdrew support last week over a hospital ward closure, has vowed he will not be held to ransom by Eurosceptics intent on making trouble.
Conservative rebel Teresa Gorman has called for a referendum on whether Britain should quit the EU and promised she would introduce a bill in parliament next month.
Major, whose government trails the opposition Labour Party by almost 40 points in opinion polls, must call an election by next May.
He will face calls for further integration from other European leaders at at an EU summit in Dublin this weekend.
Asked by a BBC interviewer if the government would maintain its "wait and see" policy on the single currency during an election campaign, Clarke said: "Yes of course, I think it is a sensible policy.
"At the moment we don't even know whether it will go ahead, we don't know which countries which will be in it. I don't think it will go ahead on January 1, 1999, necessarily."
Clarke pointed to the advantages of joining a single currency, such as trading without foreign exchange uncertainties and costs, and possibly lower interest rates.

"But there are snags, on the other hand. If there is a political charge on an unrealistic timetable to get a lot of countries into this EMU and they are not genuinely convergent ...then I would personally be against it."
"But we must keep the option open of going in," Clarke insisted
Both the Conservatives and Labour have pledged to stage a referendum on joining a single currency after the next election if the government first agrees Britain should join.
